title: Rahab Hides the Spies in Jericho
summary: Joshua sends two spies from Shittim to Jericho, where they stay at the house of a prostitute named Rahab. When the king demands the men, Rahab hides them on her roof and sends the pursuers away on a false trail. She confesses that the LORD is God in heaven and on earth, asks the spies to spare her family, and lets them down through her window in the city wall. They promise safety for everyone inside her house if she ties a scarlet cord in the window, and they return to report that the land's people are melting in fear.
story: Joshua has received God's command to cross the Jordan and has told the people to prepare. Before crossing, he sends spies, just as Moses once sent twelve men into Canaan (Numbers 13). That earlier mission ended in fear and forty years of wandering, because ten of the spies reported that the people of the land were too strong. This mission ends the opposite way: the spies return saying that the people of the land are terrified of Israel. The chapter's surprise is who makes the difference. It is not a warrior or a priest but a Canaanite prostitute who has heard what the LORD did and believes it. Rahab's story sets up the fall of Jericho in chapter 6, where she and her family are spared.
historical:
Shittim (verse 1), whose name means acacias, was Israel's last camp east of the Jordan, on the plains of Moab (Numbers 25:1). Jericho lay a few miles west of the river, an oasis city fed by a strong spring, controlling the route from the Jordan valley up into the central hill country. It is identified with Tell es-Sultan near the modern town of Jericho. The site is among the oldest continuously settled places known, with walls going back thousands of years before Joshua. Whether and how the city was occupied in the Late Bronze Age is disputed among archaeologists (see the introduction to Joshua).

Rahab mentions the drying up of the Red Sea (the exodus crossing) and the defeat of Sihon and Og, the Amorite kings east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21-35). News of these events had spread along the trade routes, and the Canaanite cities understood their implications. The mention of a king of Jericho fits what we know of Late Bronze Canaan, where each walled town typically had its own ruler.
cultural:
Houses built into or against city walls were common in ancient fortified towns, and some cities used a casemate wall, two parallel walls with rooms between them, in which people could live. Rahab's house was part of the wall, so a window opened to the outside. Flat roofs were used for work and storage, and stalks of flax (verse 6) were laid out to dry there before being processed into linen. Harvest in the Jordan valley came in spring, which fits the timing of the crossing at Passover (4:19, 5:10).

Why spies would go to a prostitute's house has been discussed since ancient times. Such a house was a place where strangers could come and go without drawing attention, and some scholars suggest it may also have served as an inn; ancient Jewish interpreters sometimes described Rahab as an innkeeper. The Hebrew word, however, is the ordinary word for a prostitute, and the New Testament keeps that description (Hebrews 11:31, James 2:25). Rahab's appeal rests on hesed (verse 12), the loyal kindness expected between parties bound by an oath, and on an oath sworn in the LORD's name. In the ancient world such oaths were binding and invoked the gods as witnesses and enforcers, which is why the spies carefully define the conditions under which they will be released from it.
literary: The chapter is a tightly told story full of suspense, irony, and reversals. The king's men search the country while the spies hide above their heads. The powerful king is fooled by a woman whose trade put her at the edge of society. The scouts, who were sent to gather information, learn most of what they need from Rahab's speech. That speech (verses 9-13) is the theological center of the chapter. It moves from what she knows (the LORD has given you the land) to what she has heard (the Red Sea, Sihon and Og) to what she confesses (the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below) to what she asks (kindness for kindness). Her confession echoes Moses' words in Deuteronomy 4:39. The repeated phrase melting in fear (verses 9, 11, 24) frames the chapter and shows the spies' final report as a direct echo of Rahab's words.

outline.t: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho
Rahab hides the spies and misleads the king's men
Rahab's confession and request for kindness
The escape through the window and the scarlet cord
The spies return with a report of fear

doctrines.note: Rahab has seen no miracle; she has only heard reports. Yet she draws the right conclusion about who the LORD is and acts on it at great risk. Hebrews 11:31 lists her among the heroes of faith.

A Canaanite, under the judgment coming on her city, is spared along with her household because she turns to the God of Israel. The chapter shows mercy reaching beyond Israel's borders to those who seek it.

Rahab heard of God's works from afar and responded. God's acts in history were meant to make his name known among the nations, as Joshua 4:24 later says, and Rahab is an early example of that witness bearing fruit.

words.note: Hesed, often translated kindness, steadfast love, or loyal love. It describes faithfulness within a relationship, going beyond the minimum required. Rahab asks the spies to show hesed because she has shown it (verse 12). The word is used most often of God's covenant love for Israel, and here it binds a Canaanite family to Israel's future.

Tiqvah, cord. The same Hebrew word also means hope elsewhere in the Old Testament, probably from the idea of a cord stretched out or waited on. The two senses are likely separate uses of one root, and one should be careful not to build too much on the pun, though some readers have found it evocative.

Masas, to melt or dissolve. The hearts of Jericho's people melt in fear (verses 9, 11, 24). The image recurs in 5:1 and ironically in 7:5, when Israel's own heart melts after defeat at Ai. Courage and fear in Joshua depend on whether God is fighting for or against a people.

Rahab, meaning wide or broad. She is one of the few Canaanites named in the book and the only one remembered with honor in later Scripture, appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus and in Hebrews and James.

christ: Rahab appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:5, as the mother of Boaz, who married Ruth. Matthew includes her deliberately, along with Tamar, Ruth, and Bathsheba, women whose stories involved scandal or foreign birth, showing that the line of the Messiah was never a tidy or exclusive one. Hebrews 11:31 praises her faith: “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.” James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of living faith. Some early Christian writers saw the scarlet cord as a picture of Christ's blood, recalling the blood on the doorposts at Passover. The New Testament itself does not make that connection, and it is better treated as a devotional reflection than as the text's intended meaning. What the New Testament does stress is that an outsider was welcomed into God's people through faith, a pattern the gospel extends to all nations.

hard.q: Rahab lied to protect the spies. Does the Bible approve of lying?
hard.a: The chapter reports Rahab's deception without comment, and the New Testament praises her faith and her hospitality to the spies, not her lie as such. Christians have answered the question in several ways. Augustine argued that lying is always wrong and that Rahab was commended for her kindness and faith despite the lie, not because of it; this view emphasizes that she was a new believer still learning God's ways. Others argue that deceiving an enemy engaged in unjust violence is not the kind of lie the ninth commandment forbids, pointing to the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1 who deceived Pharaoh and were blessed by God. This question reappears in later ethical debates, such as hiding refugees from persecutors. Readers on both sides agree that the text's focus is Rahab's faith and courage, and that her story is not a general endorsement of deception.

questions: Rahab believed based only on what she had heard. What have you heard about God that calls for a response?
The person who helps Israel most in this chapter is someone many would have written off. Whom might you be overlooking as a possible witness to God's work?
Rahab risked everything by siding with Israel's God. What would it cost you to act fully on what you believe?
